artworks.description: Although it was smaller than other centers, the Jizhou kiln complex in Jiangxi Province was among the most enterprising in Chinese history. Variegated black and brown glazes and stylized flowers—made using cut paper, which disintegrated during firing—fill the interior surface of this tea bowl, while the exterior is glazed with an additional pattern that was termed "tortoiseshell" by connoisseurs in fifteenth-century Japan.

artworks.creditLine: Yung G. Wang Family Endowment Fund
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Characterized by the use of white slip and inlaid and stamped designs, Buncheong ware is a uniquely Korean ceramic type that was produced in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Buncheong wares were used ceremonially at the court, in temples, and as tablewares. This jar shape is often called a "placenta jar," suggesting that it served a ceremonial function during childbirth. It remains unclear whether the shape was designed for that purpose or was originally intended for wine or grain storage.

artworks.title: Eagle-Owl Pendant
artworks.creditLine: Lent by the Peabody Museum of Natural History, YPM ANT 295357
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Pendants in the shape of eagles or eagle-owl hybrids probably served a ritualistic and protective role in the early Hongshan culture in China. They are made of nephrite, which was the only jade type used in China until the eighteenth century, when Burmese jade, or jadeite, also began to be imported.

artworks.title: Tripod Vessel (Gui)
artworks.creditLine: Leonard C. Hanna, Jr., Class of 1913, Fund
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Dawenkou refers both to an archaeological site and a Neolithic culture that was based along the eastern seaboard of China, particularly in the Shandong and Anhui Provinces. Ceramics from this culture are thinly potted and are burnished or rubbed rather than painted. The angular mouth and ridged design on this piece echo early examples of sheet metalwork in both shape and construction. Similar vessels were also produced in China during the Bronze Age.

artworks.dimensions:

Inner Diameter: 1 3/4 in. (4.5 cm)

artworks.description: Found in some of China’s earliest cultures and often placed on or alongside the deceased during burials, circular disks, or bi , originally symbolized the sky revolving around a central axis, referring to the belief that the heavens were divine. Over time, however, such disks became more decorative than symbolic in function.

artworks.title: Deep Bowl
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Rosemarie and Leighton R. Longhi, B.A. 1967
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Earthenware vessels from the Jomon, or cord-impressed, period are known for their surface decoration, which was created by pressing a rope onto a clay body before firing. By the middle of this period, the technique yielded elaborate three-dimensional designs such as those seen on this spectacular bowl, including appliqués on the body and four crests protruding from the rim. Although initially believed to serve a ceremonial purpose, jars of this type have been found in archaeological contexts that suggest they may also have had an everyday function.

artworks.title: Stem Cup
artworks.medium: Earthenware with burnished surface and cut decoration
artworks.creditLine: Leonard C. Hanna, Jr., Class of 1913, Fund
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Tall, elegant cups such as this one were probably intended for ritual use. They were produced by both the Dawenkou and the Longshan culture, which was also based in the Shandong Province and showed a preference for black pottery.

artworks.title: Jar
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Alice and Nasli Heeramaneck in memory of Viola and William B. Arvine
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Because preliterate societies left no writings, pottery serves as one of the primary markers for identifying an early culture and distinguishing it from others. The shape of this jar and the swirling patterns on the upper part of the body typify works produced in the northwest during the Majiayao, a variant of the Yangshao culture centered in north-central China. Thousands of jars like this one have been excavated from tombs, which may indicate that they were used for everyday activities. This jar is painted with a water mixture made from the same clay that was used for the body, though the paint was tinted with iron and manganese to create red and black. The lower part of the jar is unadorned, as it was placed partially in the ground for stability. The lugs at the sides supported a rope to carry the vessel.

artworks.description: This cast-copper anthropomorphic figure, characterized by a large head, curled arms, and fishtail-like legs, is one of the most enigmatic objects to have been unearthed among the ancient copper hoards near the Ganges River. The hoards also included celts, harpoons, and other implements. Most likely, this figure had a religious or protective function.

artworks.title: Food Vessel (Ding)
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Bequest of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Early Chinese bronze vessels were cast using a distinctive piece-mold technology, in which several ceramic pieces were carved individually and assembled around a clay core. The space between the inner core and the molds was then filled with molten bronze, and after the bronze dried, the ceramic core and molds were removed. The dense decoration and interlocking designs on this example were carved into the clay molds in reverse, so that they would read properly on the completed vessel.

artworks.title: Food Vessel (Ding)
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Gift of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The two circular eyes in the center of this cauldron are part of a zoomorphic face that also includes two curling horns and a snout. Known as a taotie , this design is ubiquitous on Chinese ritual bronzes made during the Shang and Zhou dynasties. It is often, but not conclusively, identified as a protective figure.

artworks.title: Wine Beaker (Gu)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Jonathan A. Wright in honor of Arthur F. and Mary Clabaugh Wright
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Many Chinese ritual bronze shapes can be traced to earlier examples in pottery, including the tall beaker ( gu ), which held rice wine. Access to such vessels during the Shang dynasty was limited to rulers and the elite, who used them to communicate with ancestors in ceremonies, and as goods for their tombs. The number and types of vessels placed in a tomb were marks of status, and gu beakers were among the most ubiquitous. The gu shape remained important throughout Chinese history, and vessels in the shape were made in bronze, clay, and jade. Over time, the gu became a display item and a flower vase, though the allusion to its earlier ritual function endured.

artworks.title: Ritual Serving Vessel, known as the “Song Gui”
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Wilson P. Foss, Jr., Ph.B. 1913
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Horned animal heads decorate the handles and feet of this serving vessel, and the cover can be turned over for use as a platter. A 152-character inscription, cast on the underside and inside the cover, explains that the vessel was made by the order of King Mu of Zhou, the fifth king of the Zhou dynasty, to commemorate his audience with a distinguished individual named Song, and it lists the gifts he presented to him. This inscription ends with a dedication in which Song extolls the king's benificence, and explains that this vessel we intended for use during sacrifices in honor of Song's deceased parents. It was once part of a set of ritual vessels bearing similar inscriptions.

artworks.title: Mirror
artworks.dimensions:
other: 2 1/2 in. (6.4 cm)
other (Loop): 3/4 in. (1.9 cm)
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Gift of Mrs. William H. Moore

artworks.description: The earliest Chinese mirror in the Gallery’s collection, this example features a standing hunter and six very stylized birds on the back. Though this imagery is derived from daily life, it may also have had a symbolic meaning; hunting provided food and thus was necessary for the health and stability of the community.

artworks.description: The use of four animals to represent the four cardinal directions had become an important motif in Chinese art by the beginning of the Han dynasty. The dragon symbolizes the east; the phoenix—or vermilion bird—the south; the tiger, the west; and the turtle, the north.

artworks.description: Identified by its single horn, the tianlu is one of two chimeralike beasts that were believed to be protective and auspicious and became popular in Chinese art and literature during the Han dynasty. A small cover on the back of this vessel opens, suggesting that this charming bronze may have been used as an oil lamp.

artworks.title: Mirror with a Cosmological Design
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Schuyler V.R. Cammann, B.A. 1935
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The dating of this mirror derives from the inscription cast in the outer border, which extols its beauty and explains that it was produced during the short-lived Xin dynasty with copper mined from Danyang in Jiangsu Province, noted for its mineral wealth. The design shows a central square aligned with the four cardinal directions. It represents a diagram of the cosmos as it was understood in early China. The T-, L-, and V-shaped motifs come from patterns found on the board used to play liubo , the ancestor of all battle board games.

artworks.title: Ascetic
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Winthrop and Jane Sargeant
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Once part of a larger narrative showing scenes from the lifetime of the historical Buddha, this figure’s lack of adornment and beard indicate that the sculpture represents an ascetic. Prior to developing his own path toward enlightenment—which he called the "Middle Way"—the historical Buddha Shakyamuni practiced different types of physical and mental austerities that were widespread throughout India.

artworks.title: Two-Story Tower with a Moat
artworks.medium: Earthenware with light green lead-fluxed glaze
artworks.creditLine: The Schloss Collection, Gift of Simone Schloss
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Produced in large numbers during the Han dynasty, clay models of towers and other buildings were created for inclusion in tombs. They belong to a category known as spirit goods ( mingqi ), which were made specifically for burials and intended to serve the deceased in the afterlife. Tall towers and moats such as this example replicated structures found on wealthy estates, which defined property borders and helped provide protection to landowners.

artworks.title: Farm House
artworks.creditLine: The Schloss Collection, Gift of Simone Schloss
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.

artworks.title: Footprints of the Buddha (Buddhapada)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of the Rubin-Ladd Foundation under the bequest of Ester R. Portnow
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: In this relief, auspicious motifs such as wheels, swastikas, and shrivastas (wheels with hornlike tops) fill the soles and toes of the Buddha’s footprint. The snakelike heads of the two devotees in the niches on either side indicate that they are semi-divinities; the male figure on the left is a naga , and his female counterpart, a nagini , is on the right.

artworks.title: Relief with Musicians and Dancers
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Fred Olsen
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Amid acanthus leaves and an elaborate column, a musician at center plays a handheld drum while, at right, a dancer steps in time to its rhythm, clapping his hands to the music. This relief would once have adorned the steps of a stupa, a domed structure that housed the relics of the Buddha. Although music and dance were thought to be inappropriate behaviors for the monks who prayed and practiced meditation together at stupas, the lively scene most likely reflects the activities of other visitors to the site, possibly as a precursor to more formal worship, such as ritual processions around the stupa.

artworks.title: Jar
artworks.creditLine: Leonard C. Hanna, Jr., Class of 1913, Fund
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Unlike the inhabitants of Japan during the preceding Jomon period, those of the Yayoi lived a more settled existence, due to the introduction of irrigated rice cultivation and metallurgy from the East Asian mainland. Pottery made during this period—which is defined by smooth surfaces, clean lines, and little or no decoration—differs noticeably from earlier examples, suggesting that Yayoi ceramic objects played more of a functional than ceremonial role.

artworks.title: House with a Courtyard
artworks.medium: Stoneware with incised and carved decoration
artworks.creditLine: Gift of John Hadley Cox, B.A. 1935
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: This single-story house, with an attached courtyard for animals, was produced in southern China for a tomb and is a rare example of a burial good from that region. Made in Hunan Province, this type of object depicts architecture still found in southern China and Vietnam today.

artworks.title: Mirror with the Queen Mother of the West ( Xiwangmu) and the King Father of the East (Dongwanggong)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Schuyler V.R. Cammann, B.A. 1935
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The popularity of the Queen Mother of the West, who inhabited an immortal realm located somewhere in the mysterious west and dispensed blessings such as longevity and prosperity, can be traced back to the second century B.C.E. Both she and her consort, the King Father of the East, were depicted often—and in all media—during the Han dynasty.

artworks.title: The Great Departure of the Buddha
artworks.creditLine: Purchase for the George C. Barclay Collection from the Blanche Barclay Credit
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: "The Great Departure" illustrates the moment when the historical Buddha Shakyamuni rejected his palatial home and snuck out in the middle of the night to begin his long and arduous search for enlightenment.

artworks.title: Attack of Mara
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Georgia and Michael de Havenon, B.A. 1962
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: After he revived himself following years of austerity, the historical Buddha Shakyamuni sat beneath a tree and vowed to meditate until he became enlightened. The two figures on this relief, one lay and one monastic, were part of a larger narrative showing the attack instigated by the demon Mara in a vain attempt to distract Shakyamuni and stop him from achieving enlightenment. The two demonic faces and the elephant at the top represent the members of Mara’s gang.

artworks.title: Pair of panels with semi-divinities known as yakshis
artworks.creditLine: Purchased with a gift from the John and Evelyn Kossak Foundation, Inc.
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Known as yakshis, beautiful women symbolizing the powers of nature and the earth appear in all Indian religious traditions, including Buddhism. The gestures of the women and the leaves clutched in their hands refer to the long-standing belief that the touch of a fertile young woman can cause a tree to blossom spontaneously.

artworks.title: Gandharan male figure from a relief
artworks.creditLine: Bequest of Charles E. Rogers, B.A. 1937, M.A. 1942, M.A 1982
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The clasped hands indicate devotion, which suggests that this individual—who wears lay clothing in addition to an elaborate headdress—represents a devotee. The relief was most likely once part of a larger scene, presumably a narrative from the life of the historical Buddha Shakyamuni.

artworks.description: Small, plump beings that decorate the exteriors of temples and other buildings in India are often generically termed gana, a Sanskrit word that means "group" or "assembly." These figures frequently appear in Indian art as attendants, particularly to the great Hindu god Shiva.

artworks.title: Tile with Ascetics, Figures on Balconies, and Ducks
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Evelyn Kranes Kossak
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: This image, showing two ascetics practicing while others converse on a balcony and waterfowl frolic in a lotus pond, is typical of the tiles that once decorated the sides of an apsidal temple at the site of Harwan in the Kashmir region. Representations of naked and emaciated practitioners are not generally found in contemporaneous Buddhist imagery outside of Harwan, which suggests that the site may illustrate the melding of earlier traditions with others that led to the development of later esoteric Buddhism, known for its more austere practices.

artworks.creditLine: Lent by the Peabody Museum of Natural History, YPM ANT 295688
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: In Korea, comma-shaped ornaments decorated belts, crowns, necklaces, and bracelets. This bracelet combines quartz with forty-two small, dark blue glass beads. Known as Indo-Pacific beads, they were made in southern India for trade to Southeast Asia and beyond. Thousands of these glass beads have been excavated in Korea, attesting to the importance of maritime trade to Silla, which was located in the southern part of the peninsula.

artworks.title: Court Official
artworks.medium: Earthenware with traces of slip and pigment
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Maitland F. Griggs, B.A. 1896
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The height of this figure and its long, narrow physique indicate that it once graced an elite tomb in or near the city of Luoyang, which was established as the capital of the Northern Wei dynasty in the late fifth century C.E. The tall, conical hat and high-waisted robe typify court attire worn by civil and other officials. The long sword suggests that this figure, who is not wearing armor, was tasked with overseeing the military. This sculpture was part of a retinue of retainers and officials placed in a tomb as attendants to the deceased.

artworks.title: Flat Bottle
artworks.medium: Stoneware with raised decoration and natural ash glaze (Sue ware)
artworks.creditLine: Leonard C. Hanna, Jr., Class of 1913, Fund
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: First produced in the mid-fifth century C.E., Sue ware, which is thin and hard, was fired at temperatures ranging from 1,100 to 1,200 degrees Celsius. The production of Sue ware developed in response to the trade of Korean ceramics to Japan and marked the first use of a pottery wheel by Japanese artists. The glaze on the surface of this bottle is accidental and appeared during firing.

artworks.title: Standing Female
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Rosemarie and Leighton R. Longhi, B.A. 1967
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Haniwa (ring of clay) statues are unglazed earthenware sculptures that were made between the third and the sixth century C.E., primarily to protect grave mounds from erosion or to mark burial sites. Though they originally took the form of simple cylinders, by the fourth century haniwa also included human figures, animals, and occasionally architectural structures. This example includes a female figure sculpted on the top of the typical haniwa cylinder, which would be buried in the ground. She has two looped bows on her dress and one remaining earring on the left side of her head. The round clay pieces attached to her neckline appear to be remnants of a necklace, suggesting that she represents a shrine maiden known as a miko. Figures of such maidens were the most popular haniwa sculptures, due to the status of the maidens in Japan at that time.

artworks.title: Duck
artworks.creditLine: Lent by the Peabody Museum of Natural History, YPM ANT 148348
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.

artworks.title: Guardian with a Shield
artworks.medium: Earthenware with slip and traces of black and red pigment
artworks.creditLine: Purchased with an anonymous gift and the Leonard C. Hanna, Jr., Class of 1913, Fund
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Tomb sculptures holding oversize shields belong to a subset of guardians produced in the northeast during the mid-sixth century C.E. Often made in pairs, they were placed at or near the entrance of a tomb to protect the space and its inhabitants.

artworks.title: Granary with Thatched Roof
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Rosemarie and Leighton R. Longhi, B.A. 1967
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: While the majority of haniwa statues depict figures and animals, at times they also take the form of houses and other architectural structures. This example has a thatched roof and a single door but lacks air vents, which points to its representation as a granary or some other storage facility.

Her dress, consisting of a long skirt in alternating colors and a long-sleeved blouse under a jacket, was very fashionable in China in the seventh century C.E.—as well as in Korea and Japan.

Her dress, consisting of a long skirt in alternating colors and a long-sleeved blouse under a jacket, was very fashionable in China in the seventh century C.E.—as well as in Korea and Japan.

artworks.medium: Stoneware with white slip and glaze
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. George Hopper Fitch, B.A. 1932
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: This vase was used to transport wine, and its shape echoes that of amphorae made throughout the eastern Mediterranean. The dragon handles and the flat bottom, however, attest to the adaptation of this vessel in China.

artworks.title: Jar

artworks.title: Mirror with Animals and Grapes
artworks.creditLine: In memory of Dr. Bert G. and Florence O. Anderson
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Grapes were introduced to China from the western reaches of Central Asia beginning in the Han dynasty. They were particularly treasured during the Tang period, when grape wine became popular at court and among the gentry. Mirrors depicting grapes and animals—often identified as lions, another exoticism—were popular in the seventh and eighth centuries C.E., the height of multinational trade between China and the Mediterranean world that took place along the overland routes known collectively as the Silk Road.

artworks.title: Bowing Figure
artworks.medium: Earthenware with slip and traces of pigment
artworks.creditLine: Gift of H. Christopher Luce, B.A. 1972, in honor of Henry R. Luce, B.A. 1920
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Examples of bowing figures wearing court clothing are rare and found primarily in imperial or aristocratic tombs. They illustrate a moment at the court when an individual would bow to his supervisor before beginning his duties.

artworks.title: Buddha
artworks.creditLine: Lent by Steven M. Kossak, B.A. 1972
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.

artworks.title: Court Lady
artworks.medium: Earthenware with slip and traces of pigment
artworks.creditLine: Gift of the Associates in Fine Arts
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: A new concept of beauty, featuring full-figured women with elaborate hairstyles, emerged in China in the early eighth century C.E. This change has often been associated with Yang Guifei, the beloved and influential concubine of the emperor Xuanzong (r. 713–56 C.E.). While Yang rose to power in the 740s, evidence of the taste for voluptuous women appears in tombs that date as early as the 720s.

artworks.title: Jar
artworks.creditLine: Wayland Wells Williams, B.A. 1910, Collection, Gift of Mrs. Frances Wayland Williams
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The dark blue glaze covering this jar derives from cobalt, an oxide ore that was later used as a pigment for blue-and-white porcelain—the development of which in the mid-fourteenth century changed the course of global ceramic history. Mines in the Henan and Gansu Provinces may have been the source for the native cobalt that first decorated funerary and trade ceramics in the eighth and ninth centuries C.E.

artworks.title: Mirror with Four Fabulous Animals Representing the Four Directions
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Schuyler V.R. Cammann, B.A. 1935
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The use of four animals to represent the four cardinal directions had become an important motif in Chinese art by the beginning of the Han dynasty. The dragon symbolizes the east; the phoenix—or vermilion bird—the south; the tiger, the west; and the turtle, the north.

artworks.title: Horse
artworks.creditLine: Gift of H. Christopher Luce, B.A. 1972, in honor of Henry R. Luce, B.A. 1920
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The bright, multicolored glazes covering the surface of this horse illustrate the development of the three-color, or sancai, tradition in China in the late seventh and early eighth centuries C.E. Various combinations of amber, green, and white glazes decorate ceramic models and vessels found exclusively in imperial and aristocratic tombs. The acquisition of long-legged horses from the region of present-day Afghanistan—which were faster and more maneuverable than the smaller native species—was a preoccupation of the ruling elite, who also included clay representations of these animals in their tombs.

artworks.title: Bottle with Roundels

artworks.description: The technique of fusing two blown-glass elements, known as incalmo , is one of the many innovations in glass technology made during the Abbasid period. Here, dark blue glass has been fused with green.

artworks.title: Mirror with Birds, a Dragon, and a Rabbit
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Schuyler V.R. Cammann, B.A. 1935
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: At the top of this mirror, a rabbit mixes the elixir of immortality beneath a cassia tree, a reference to the animal’s position as an attendant to Chang E, the goddess of long life who inhabited the moon. The dragon pictured in the waves at the bottom is another traditional East Asian symbol, while the two birds on either side with ribbons in their mouths reflect interactions with West Asia. This Sasanian motif reached China from Iran via trade on the fabled overland Silk Road, which linked China to the Mediterranean world.

artworks.title: Bactrian Camel
artworks.creditLine: Gift of H. Christopher Luce, B.A. 1972, in honor of Henry R. Luce, B.A. 1920
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Although not native to China, camels played a significant role in the extensive overland trade that linked China to the eastern Mediterranean, and they were a common sight in major urban centers. In Tang-dynasty tombs, clay camels were paired with sculptures of West Asian grooms, a reference to both this important trade route and the status of the deceased, who could afford foreign servants and animals.

artworks.title: Bowl with an Arabic Inscription and Palmettes
artworks.medium: Earthenware with cobalt blue over opaque white glaze
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Gift of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Written in cobalt blue, the inscription reads “Blessings to the owner, made by.” Other bowls of this type were signed by the artists, which speaks to the recognition awarded to potters in Iraq in the ninth and tenth centuries C.E.. This bowl might have been signed at the time of purchase, thereby enhancing its value. The use of a white glaze to cover the yellowish-gray pottery body, and that of cobalt blue, appears in Basra in Iraq in the early ninth century C.E. in response to white wares from China, some of which were also painted with cobalt blue.

artworks.title: Box with a Floral Design
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Bequest of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The delicate, six-petal flowers on the top of this box were created using a resist-wax technique that was adapted from textile production. The blue glaze was derived from cobalt, and its presence helps date the box to the early eighth century C.E., when blue was commonly added to the amber, green, and white glazes that originally defined three-color, or sancai, ware.

artworks.title: Lobed Dish
artworks.creditLine: Edward H. Dunlap, B.A. 1934, Fund
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The shape of this dish derives from silver and attests to the influence of domestic and imported metalwork in China during the Tang dynasty. Small white dishes such as this example were traded by land and sea to West Asia and had a profound impact on early Islamic ceramics. Valued for their similarity to pearls, Chinese white wares were imitated at ceramic centers in Basra (present-day Iraq) and elsewhere.

artworks.title: Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara with Six Arms

artworks.title: Bowl
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Gift of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Ceramics with marbling, created by melding clays of assorted colors into the shape of a bowl, first appear in the repertory of Chinese ceramics in the ninth and tenth centuries. They were produced only in north China, and in small numbers, until around the eleventh or twelfth century. The invention of marble wares illustrates the constant experimentation and innovation found in the Chinese ceramics industry from the ninth to the fourteenth century. The animal-print-like designs seen here echo patterns found in earlier Roman glass, (see 1955.6.17) one of the most desired luxury goods in the ancient world that was traded to China as early as the second and third centuries.

artworks.title: Bowl
artworks.medium: Earthenware with lustre on opaque glaze
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Gift of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The white glaze covering the buff-colored clay of this bowl is another example of the Iraqi interest in replicating early Chinese whitewares (see 1983.68). The brown and amber luster, derived from mixing metallic components such as ground copper and silver into a glaze and firing it for a second time in a kiln in which the oxygen has been reduced, is an Iraqi innovation that spread throughout the Islamic world and ultimately around the globe. The circles in the design illustrate flowering bushes in early Iraqi ceramics, and it is likely that the diagonal lines are also intended to represent stylized foliage.

artworks.title: Bowl with Splashes
artworks.medium: Earthenware splash-painted on opaque white glaze
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Gift of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The flowing blue and green lines on this bowl are a response to imported Chinese ceramics that were often decorated with splashed glazes in shades of white, green, and amber. The shape of the bowl and the use of an opaque white ground to cover the body also echo imported Chinese wares, in particular early porcelains traded to West Asia in the late eighth and ninth centuries C.E.

artworks.title: Jar
artworks.creditLine: Anonymous gift in memory of Pauline H. Lee
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Controlled by the Heian government, the complex at Sanage, near Nagoya, had over one thousand kilns and was the major center for the production of glazed ceramics during the Heian period. Sanage ware was inspired by imported Korean pieces, and production began in the preceding Nara period, marking the creation of the earliest glazed ceramics in Japan.

artworks.title: The Hindu God Hari Hara (Combination of Shiva and Vishnu)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Lindsay Harper Makepeace in honor of LeRoy McKim Makepeace, B.A. 1937

artworks.title: Hindu God Ganesha
artworks.creditLine: Gift of John D. Viener, B.A. 1961
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: One of the most popular gods in Hinduism, Ganesha acquired his characteristic elephant head when his father, the god Shiva, accidentally beheaded him and was forced by his mother, the goddess Parvati, to replace Ganesha’s missing head. In this piece, the placement of Ganesha’s bent legs suggests that he is dancing. He holds an ax in his upper right hand, an attribute that illustrates his ability to cut through illusions, and there is a small image of a rat, Ganesha’s mount, on the front of the rectangular plinth.

artworks.title: Hindu Goddess Lakshmi with Elephants (Gajalakshmi)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of the Rubin-Ladd Foundation under the bequest of Ester R. Portnow

artworks.title: Box
artworks.creditLine: Wayland Wells Williams, B.A. 1910, Collection, Gift of Mrs. Frances Wayland Williams
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Ceramics with green, gray-green, and blue-green glazes are often classified as "celadons" in Western writings. Traditionally, the term has been understood as a reference to a character in an eighteenth-century French play; however, it may have been derived from a corruption of the name Saladin, the founder of the short-lived Ayyubid dynasty in Egypt, who sent forty green-glazed ceramic pieces to a Syrian ruler in the twelfth century. The gray-green glaze on this box is characteristic of Yue wares produced in Zhejiang Province from the ninth to the eleventh century for use at court and for domestic consumption.

artworks.description: The flaming jewel held in the figure’s upraised left hand indicates that this sculpture represents either Kshitigarbha, the Bodhisattva of the Earth Matrix (in Chinese, Dizang), or Avalokiteshvara (in Chinese, Guanyin). Both hold such a jewel in several of their many manifestations.

artworks.description: One of eight directional guardians that were traditionally placed at the corners of a temple, this protector wears a crown indicating that he once adorned a temple dedicated to Vishnu, one of the three primary gods of Hinduism.

artworks.title: Bowl with Bird
artworks.medium: Earthenware with pigments on slip underglaze (Nishapur ware)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Fred Olsen
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The delicate yellow pigment used in the decoration of this small bowl derives from antimony; it is unique to ceramics produced in the Nishapur region in the east of present-day Iran, one of the great ceramic centers in the tenth and eleventh centuries. The central standing bird and the sprig of flowers in its beak illustrate the continuation of imagery from the Sasanian period (224–651 C.E.) in early Islamic ceramics. The pseudowriting in the band around the bird reflects the role of calligraphy as an artistic motif in early Islamic art (see 1954.53.15).

artworks.title: Votive Plaque with Budhha Seated in the Bodh Gaya Temple
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Jai K. Chandrasekhar, B.A. 1987, J.D. 1997
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The shape of the tower, and the lowered right hand of the Buddha seated inside it, indicate that this plaque represents the Historical Buddha Shakyamuni at Bodh Gaya in India. A famous temple marking the location of this momentous event, Bodh Gaya was one of the most important sites for practice and pilgrimage from the ninth to the twelfth century. Images of the temple are prevalent in votive plaques such as this one, which were made throughout Buddhist Asia to serve as both offerings and souvenirs.

artworks.title: Attendant to a Hindu God
artworks.creditLine: Lent by Michael de Havenon, B.A. 1962, and Georgia de Havenon
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The frontal posture of this figure and its raised right hand, which holds an offering, indicate that it served as an attendant to an important Hindu god such as Shiva or Vishnu. The lowered left hand suggests that it would have once stood to the right of the primary icon, with another comparable attendant placed at the left.

artworks.title: Standing Jizo Bosatsu
artworks.medium: Single block of cypress wood with linen, gesso, lacquer, and gilding
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Rosemarie and Leighton R. Longhi, B.A. 1967
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Important in East Asian Buddhist practices and known in Japanese as Jizō, Kshitigarbha is the Bodhisattva of the Earth Womb and is revered as a protector who relieves suffering and saves souls from hell. Unlike other bodhisattvas, he is depicted wearing monastic clothing and often holds a wish-granting jewel in his upraised left hand.

artworks.title: Portrait of Zhu Guan, from the set Five Old Men of Suiyang
artworks.medium: Album leaf; ink and color on silk
artworks.dimensions:
without mounting: 15 7/8 × 12 11/16 in. (40.3 × 32.2 cm)
with mounting: 24 × 18 7/8 in. (61 × 47.9 cm)
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Gift of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Sometime in the early 1050s, five portraits were painted to commemorate the lives of five scholar-officials who had all reached old age and retired to live in Suiyang. Du Yan, who had attained the rank of prime minister, the highest rank among the five, was just eighty; he retired in 1051. Zhu Guan, shown here, a native of Suiyang, had risen to be the Director of the Ministry of War; he was eighty-eight. Each portrait showed considerable attention to facial detail, and the figures were depicted in a formal standing pose, indicative of each man's virtue, and wearing informal robes and scholar's hats. The portraits and the colophons that made up the original scroll are now divided among several museums. The colophons range from 1056 to 1898 making the Five Old Men of Suiyang one of the most extensively documented paintings in the history of art.

artworks.title: Hindu Deities Shiva and Parvati as Uma-Maheshvara
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Michael de Havenon, B.A. 1962, and Georgia de Havenon
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: When depicted with their children Skanda and Ganesha, Shiva and Parvati are generally known as Uma-Maheshvara. The goddess Parvati is shown in her avatar as Uma, the daughter of the Himalayas, while Shiva takes the form of Maheshvara, or the "Great God."

artworks.title: Phoenix Head Vase
artworks.creditLine: Leonard C. Hanna, Jr., Class of 1913, Fund
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The phoenix head, between the lip and the top of this vase, exemplifies the endless visual dialogues that characterize Chinese and West Asian art from the ninth to the fourteenth century. Although the phoenix head is a Chinese addition that first appeared in the late seventh century, the shape of this vessel can be traced to Roman glass ewers with pinched lips (see 1955.6.218) and to West Asian metalwork produced from the sixth to the tenth century. The dark green glaze covering this large vessel is derived from lead. Boasting a long history, this glaze is found on ceramics in both West Asia (see 1952.52.3) and China (see 1948.44) during the second and third centuries C.E. In China particularly from the second to the ninth century, lead green glazes were often used on goods, both vessels and sculptures, that were placed in tombs for use by the deceased.

artworks.title: Dish
artworks.medium: Stoneware with gray-green glaze (possibly Zhanggongxiang ware)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Victor Novotny
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Subtle gray-green glazes and simple, clean shapes were valued in China during the eleventh and twelfth centuries, particularly at the court.

artworks.title: Dish with Duck Amid Clouds
artworks.medium: Stoneware with incised decoration and three-color (sancai) glaze
artworks.creditLine: Wayland Wells Williams, B.A. 1910, Collection, Gift of Mrs. Frances Wayland Williams
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The duck flitting in the center of this delightful dish derives from representations of flying birds that first appeared in metalworking traditions in West Asia during the fourth to sixth century and, later, in Chinese metalworking and clay. The three colors—green, amber, and white—continue the appearance of the fabled Chinese three-color, or sancai , glaze, which first appeared around 675 C.E. (see 2009.198.14). The green and amber colors in this glaze were used in the second and third centuries, whereas the white (see 1950.170) developed in the late sixth century, spurred in part by the color of imported silver.

artworks.title: Dish with Lions, Bulls, and Harpies
artworks.medium: Earthenware with incised decoration through slip and underglaze (Garrus ware)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Wilson P. Foss, Jr., Ph.B. 1913
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: This spectacular dish is unusual because of the lions, bulls, and harpies boldly carved into the interior and exterior. The creatures have stylized eyes, bodies, and tails and pace slowly around the center of the bowl. Lions and bulls have a long history as signifiers of power, particularly imperial strength, in West Asian traditions. The harpy, a creature with the head of a woman and the body of a bird, has parallels in early Greek and Roman as well as Indic mythology, in which such figures are called kinnaris. Greco-Roman harpies, known for their wisdom, are associated with the powers of the wind and storms. In Iran, particularly during the Seljuk period, harpies were often depicted in clay (see 1953.24.15) and other media to protect against evil; they are associated with the planet Mercury.

artworks.title: Seated Bodhisattva

artworks.description: Manjushri is identified by the manuscript on the lotus in his upraised left hand. The very stylized hair ribbons that tie his diadem to his head typify sculptures produced in the western part of Tibet during the second diffusion of Buddhism, from the tenth to the twelfth century.

artworks.description: The shape of this jar, particularly its straight sides and slightly rounded cover, echoes a type of bronze jar or bucket made during the Bronze Age in Vietnam as well as in related cultures in southern China. The technique used to render the lively lotus scroll that fills the surface of the jar is an innovation found in the vibrant Vietnamese industry in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The jar was shaped and covered with a glaze before the design was carved into the surface, inlaid with iron-brown pigment, and fired.

artworks.title: Model of the Bodh Gaya Temple
artworks.creditLine: Lent by Steven M. Kossak, B.A. 1972

artworks.description: Miniature representations of the Bodh Gaya temple were used as devotional objects and souvenirs of pilgrimages. The temple marks the location where Siddhartha Gautama achieved enlightenment, became the historical Buddha Shakyamuni, and established Buddhism.

artworks.title: Bowl
artworks.medium: Stoneware with crackled blue glaze (Jun ware)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Dr. Yale Kneeland, Jr., B.A. 1922
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Jun wares, made for the court and for popular consumption, were produced at the kilns in Henan Province from the tenth to the fifteenth century. The delicate, robin’s-egg blue glaze covering this bowl was invented at the Henan kilns and typifies early Jun wares. The richness of the glaze is enhanced by the pattern of small cracks that fills the surface, which is known as crackle or crazing. While it remains unclear whether this effect was deliberate or caused by an accident in the kiln, it was prized at the court in the twelfth century and was often recreated in later ceramics.

artworks.title: Stele of Jina Parsvanatha
artworks.creditLine: Gift of the Rubin-Ladd Foundation under the bequest of Ester R. Portnow

artworks.title: Mirror with Decoration of Flowers and Children
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Schuyler V.R. Cammann, B.A. 1935
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The four scantily clad young boys crawling along the edges of this mirror back are putti-like figures adapted from art of the eastern Mediterranean world, which arrived in China as part of the trade along the Silk Road. The lotuses they hold and the pond in the background, however, reflect the introduction of lotus imagery to China with the Indian religion of Buddhism. By the early Song dynasty, the theme of boys with lotus flowers had become popular in paintings and the three-dimensional arts, and was symbolic of the desire for generations of sons.

artworks.description: This ewer belongs to a rare type of Korean pottery painted with brown iron oxide and covered with green glaze. Crafted primarily in Jeolla Province in the southwest, these ceramics provide a link between the famed, refined celadon wares of the eleventh and twelfth centuries and the distinctive Buncheong stoneware produced after the fifteenth century, which tends toward a more unassuming style with whimsical designs.

artworks.description: The Chinese envoy Xu Jing visited Korea in 1123, and he was so impressed with Korean celadons that he compared them favorably to earlier Chinese court wares, such as those made at the Ru kilns. Ceramics with gray-green glazes were the most widely produced—and favored—wares during the Goryeo dynasty.

artworks.title: Bottle with Chrysanthemum
artworks.medium: Stoneware with incised decoration and iron-brown slip under clear glaze (Cizhou ware)
artworks.creditLine: Wayland Wells Williams, B.A. 1910, Collection, Gift of Mrs. Frances Wayland Williams
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Cizhou wares were produced in a substantial number of kilns throughout northern China, particularly from the ninth to the fourteenth century. They are named after Ci Prefecture, in southern Hebei Province, which housed concentrations of kilns producing these wares. Intended primarily for domestic distribution and use, they are noted for their bold and sturdy shapes, lively and engaging designs, and contrasting shades of white, brown, and black. On this bottle, a blossoming lotus flower was incised into the white slip covering the body. The design was further enhanced with brown pigment, derived from iron, highlighting the tips of the petals.

artworks.title: Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara in the Water-Moon Manifestation (Shuiyue Guanyin)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Winston F. C. Guest, B.A. 1927
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, known in Chinese as Guanyin, is the embodiment of the virtue of compassion and became the most important deity in Buddhism around the sixth century C.E. Represented in different manifestations and throughout Asia, Avalokiteshvara is usually identified by a small seated Buddha depicted within his headdress. This figure’s relaxed posture and raised right leg indicate that it represents the Water-Moon (Shuiyue) avatar, one of many forms taken by this popular deity in which he is seated in his personal pure land or paradise. Known as Mount Potalaka, this perfected land was originally located on an island somewhere south of India, but in Chinese traditions, the island moved to a new location off the east coast of Zhejiang Province.

artworks.title: Tea Bowl with "Hare's Fur" Design
artworks.creditLine: Wayland Wells Williams, B.A. 1910, Collection, Gift of Mrs. Frances Wayland Williams
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The iridescent surface of this tea bowl and its silvery pattern, which is known as "hare’s fur," resulted from the crystallization of the iron in the glaze during firing. Tea bowls made at Jian, as well as farther north in the Jizhou kilns, played a significant role in global ceramic history. Buddhist monks who traveled to China to study and practice brought tea bowls from these kilns back to Japan, where they became part of the tea ceremony and were often reinterpreted by Japanese potters. Known as tenmoku in the Japanese tradition, these Chinese tea bowls—and their Japanese counterparts—appeared in Europe in the late nineteenth century, where their shapes and designs were incorporated into the burgeoning studio potter movement.

artworks.title: Tea Bowl with Flowers
artworks.medium: Stoneware with paper-cut designs and black-and-brown glaze (Jizhou ware)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Dr. Howard Balensweig, B.S. 1943, and Mrs. Carolyn Balensweig
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The flowers decorating the interior of this bowl are often found on bowls produced at the Jizhou kilns, as well as at the Jian kilns farther south in Fujian Province, and are usually identified as plum blossoms, a flower that was extolled in Chinese literature and poetry. However, the inclusion of six petals on the flowers suggests that they actually represent cape jasmine, another flower that was often cited in literature, at times in association with the tradition of Chan (Zen) Buddhism.

artworks.title: Mythical Creature Tianlu
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Dr. Howard Balensweig, B.S. 1943, and Mrs. Carolyn Balensweig

artworks.description: The two nonfunctional knobs on the sides of this vase likely reference metal vessels of this shape that were used for a game known as touhu , in which arrows were shot into the neck of a vase and its two narrow openings at the sides.

artworks.title: Bowl with a Peacock
artworks.medium: Earthenware with white slip, carving, and brown and green under clear glaze
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Wilson P. Foss, Jr., Ph.B. 1913
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The defined rim of this bowl, with its dotted pattern, and the sketch rendering of the bird standing amid foliage in the center typify a ceramic type known as Aghkand ware, produced in present-day Azerbaijan and Russian Georgia. The carving on these ceramics is sometimes referred to as the incised-outline style because the bird and other elements are first carved into the white slip and then colored, usually with a combination of brown and green, as here. The use of white, brown, and green can be traced to the creation of the three-color, or sancai , glaze in Tang-period China, (see 2009.198.14) as can the technique of carving a design into clay before adding color. This technique, sometimes described using the Italian term sgraffito (meaning “to scratch”), is found in seventh- and eighth-century Chinese ceramics as well as in ninth- and tenth-century wares produced around Nishapur, in northeast Iran.

artworks.title: Mirror Depicting the Hero Ci Fei
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Gift of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The figure with an upheld sword at the prow of the boat represents Ci Fei, a Han-dynasty hero who leaped from the deck of a ship to fight a dragon and save his fellow passengers. Depictions of this tale—based on the Huainanzi , a collection of essays from the second century B.C.E.—appear in paintings from as early as the Tang dynasty, and the theme recurred in the visual arts until the twelfth century, particularly in northern China. The large, four-character inscription at the top of the mirror reads, "Great and resplendent is the heaven," a possible allusion to the grace that was inherent in Ci Fei’s sacrifice.

artworks.creditLine: Gift of David M. Levitt, B.A. 1938
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The development of new types of clay bodies in Syria in the tenth century C.E. was a response to the introduction of high-fired stonewares and porcelains from China. Made with a combination of clay, silica, and ground glass, or frit, stonepaste was widely used throughout the Islamic world. This bowl illustrates a type of ceramic known as Raqqa ware, which is named for a town in northeast Syria where some of the workshops that produced these ceramics were located. Examples were also found in Turkey and Egypt.

artworks.title: Bowl with a Rider, Hound and Two Birds
artworks.medium: Stonepaste with white slip, pigment, and gold under clear glaze (Minai ware)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of David M. Levitt

artworks.title: Bowl with an Equestrian Procession
artworks.medium: Stonepaste with pigment, enamels and gilding over opaque white glaze (Minai ware)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Fanny H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The riders circling the center of this colorful bowl may illustrate a procession or a hunt. The bowl is an example of Minai ware, a type that was produced exclusively from the last quarter of the twelfth century to the first decades of the thirteenth. Also known as seven colors ( haft rang ), Minai wares were crafted using a laborious process, in which the colors were applied at different times and with different techniques.

artworks.title: Dish
artworks.medium: Stoneware with crackled blue glaze (Jun ware)

artworks.title: Vase with Cranes and Clouds
artworks.medium: Stoneware with inlaid slip design under green glaze
artworks.creditLine: Leonard C. Hanna, Jr., Class of 1913, Fund
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The cranes and clouds were etched into the clay body of this vase and filled with white and black slip before the piece was glazed and fired. This technique was common in Korea in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, but was extremely rare in China. The shape, on the other hand, known as a maebyong in Korean, was derived from the Chinese meiping , a form that originally functioned as a bottle but was later used to display plum blossoms.

artworks.title: Dish with Lotuses
artworks.medium: Porcelain with molded under glaze decoration  (Ding ware)
artworks.creditLine: Robert Hatfield Ellsworth Fund
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Like most Chinese ceramics, Ding wares are named for the geographic region in which they were produced; they are cited in a well-known list of the five great kilns active in China during the Song dynasty (960–1127). Produced in the Dingzhou region of Hebei Province, they are characterized by their thin porcelain bodies and elegant ivory-tinged glazes. This distinctive glaze color developed after the eleventh century, when coal replaced wood as fuel for the kilns. The earliest Ding wares (see 1950.170) were covered with a glaze that had a slightly whiter hue. These early whitewares, produced in the north in the seventh to the tenth century, were among the first ceramics mentioned in Chinese and West Asian poetry; some were reserved for use by the court. The shape of this dish, as well as its dense pattern of lotus flowers and leaves, was created with a mold. The decoration illustrates the style of Ding wares produced during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The rendering of the scrolling stems and plump comma-shaped leaves parallels depictions of foliage on contemporaneous Islamic ceramics (see 1958.63.23).

artworks.description: The development of new types of clay bodies in Syria in the tenth century C.E. was a response to the introduction of high-fired stoneware and porcelain from China. Stonepaste—made with a combination of clay, silica, and ground glass or frit—first developed in Iran in the ninth century C.E. and was widely used throughout the Islamic world. This bowl is an example of Raqqa ware, a ceramic type named after a town in northeastern Syria where some of the workshops that produced these pieces were located. Raqqa ware has also been found in Turkey and Egypt.

artworks.title: Bowl with Birds
artworks.medium: Earthenware with carved decoration under clear glaze (Garrus ware)
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Gift of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Decorated with an interlaced design and a heraldic depiction of birds, this bowl belongs to a type known as Garrus ware. Named for a district southwest of the Caspian Sea where some of the first examples were found, Garrus vessels were made by covering the clay body with a slip (a cream-colored mixture of clay), then carving the designs, darkening them, and finally, applying a transparent glaze.

artworks.title: Beaker with Fleur-de-Lis
artworks.medium: Glass, free-blown with enamel and gilding
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Bequest of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The decoration on this beaker, particularly the French fleur-de-lis, indicates that it was made in Syria for an individual or for one of the governments established throughout West Asia by the European crusaders who invaded the region during the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth centuries. Glass and other luxury items were commissioned by these governments, which ultimately dissolved in the late thirteenth century due to lack of financial support from Europe, regional divisions, and the formation of the Ilkhanid Empire under the Mongols.

artworks.title: Bottle with Interlacing and Foliate Designs
artworks.medium: Stonepaste with gild and enamels over blue glaze (Lajvardina ware)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of David M. Levitt
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Known as Lajvardina ware, after the Persian word for lapis lazuli, ceramics of this type were produced in Iran only during the Ilkhanid period and for a specific, and wealthy, group of patrons. Despite the reference to lapis lazuli, the dark blue glazed background derives from cobalt ore, also used and highly valued in ceramics produced in China under Mongol rule (see ILE1984.13) in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. The dense patterning of interlaced foliage, painted over the glaze with gold, and the white and red pigments show parallels to the designs on Chinese (see new Ding dish on view) and Iranian Sultanabad wares (see 1958.63.23) produced from the twelfth to the fourteenth century. The same is true of the division of the surface into distinct horizontal registers (see 1947.69).

artworks.title: Ewer with Lotuses
artworks.medium: Stoneware with white slip and iron-brown pigment under clear glaze
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Michael de Havenon, B.A. 1962, and Georgia de Havenon

artworks.title: Celestial Being (Kinnari)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Georgia and Michael de Havenon, B.A. 1962
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Kinnari —female celestial beings that are half-human, half-bird—guard the human realm in both Buddhist and Hindu traditions.

artworks.title: Dish in the Shape of a Chrysanthemum
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Bequest of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The many small lobes defining this chrysanthemum-shaped dish are also found in lacquer and metalwork produced during the Yuan dynasty. The turquoise glaze illustrates longstanding interchanges with West Asia, where this color of glaze first appeared around the second or third century. Similar turquoise glazes often covered large ceramic transport jars, (see 1930.486) which were used to move perfumes, date oil, glass, metal, smaller ceramics, or other luxuries by sea. Examples of transport jars have been found as far west as the east coast of Africa and as far east as Japan, attesting to the breadth of maritime trade from the ninth to the fourteenth century. Turquoise first appears as a glaze and a pigment in ceramics produced in Hunan Province, in south China, around the ninth century (see 1955.4.90). It was later used, albeit sparingly, in the Cizhou kilns in the north.

artworks.title: Bowl with Inscription Reading "Good Appetite"
artworks.medium: Stonepaste with luster on opaque glaze with pigment
artworks.creditLine: Gift of David M. Levitt
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Both the stonepaste body of this dish and the use of a luster glaze continue innovations developed earlier in West Asian ceramics as part of ongoing dialogues with the Chinese industry. Stonepaste was developed in Egypt around the eleventh century. Luster (see 1951.51.19) was found first in Iraq in the ninth century, and its use spread to Egypt and Syria; it was most likely introduced by migrating artisans to Iran, particularly Kashan, in the twelfth century. Written in the Thuluth script, the Arabic inscription on this bowl illustrates the continuing importance of calligraphy in the Quran as an artistic motif in Islamic ceramics. The blue scalloped border continues the use of cobalt as a pigment and glaze colorant first found in China in the eighth century (see 1955.4.97a-b) and in West Asia (see 1951.51.65) in the ninth century.

artworks.title: Vase with Lotuses
artworks.medium: Stoneware with molded decoration under green glaze (Longquan ware)
artworks.creditLine: Hobart and Edward Small Moore Memorial Collection, Bequest of Mrs. William H. Moore
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The complex of kilns near Longquan in southern Zhejiang Province had started production during the tenth century, but it was only after the retreat of the Song court to Hangzhou in the twelfth century that Longquan became a major center of ceramic production. The Longquan wares were distinguished by their thick translucent glaze, green jade-like color and texture, and fine, light gray body. The kilns achieved a height of production during the thirteenth century, both for the domestic and the export markets. After the Mongol conquest of China and the establishment of Yuan rule, the kilns continued to produce ceramics, particularly large plates and vases for export. There was a taste for more elaborate decoration, and the potters met that demand by using mold-impressed motifs applied to the surface as seen in the floral scroll of this vase.

artworks.title: Stem cup
artworks.medium: Stoneware with iron brown spots under green glaze (Longquan ware)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Frances Wayland Williams
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.

artworks.title: Bowl with Deer
artworks.medium: Stonepaste with pigment under a clear glaze (Sultanabad ware)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of David M. Levitt
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: Although they are classified as Sultanabad ware, after the location where they were first recognized, this type of heavily potted and lushly decorated ceramics was made in Kashan, an important Iranian center for centuries. The white clay body of this dish is crafted with stonepaste, a combination of finely ground quartz, bits of glass, and a refined clay. Stonepaste was invented in Egypt in the late eleventh century, in part as a response to imported Chinese whitewares; it later spread, possibly by migrating potters, to Iran and other West Asian ceramic centers. This lush design of a seated deer surrounded by stylized petals was drawn in black and then filled with black, blue, and turquoise pigments before being enhanced by a clear glaze. The theme of a deer gazing upward at the moon first appeared in Sultanabad wares during the Ilkhanid period because of the close familial ties between its rulers and those of the Mongol Yuan dynasty in China. Such images derive from a melding of the perennial Chinese theme and tradition of moon gazing and the position of deer as recipients of the Historical Buddha’s first sermon at the Deer Park in India.

artworks.title: Plate
artworks.medium: Porcelain painted with underglaze cobalt blue
artworks.creditLine: Lent by the Peabody Museum of Natural History
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The use of cobalt blue on a porcelain body first appeared in the eighth century C.E. and is arguably the most important development in ceramic history. The flowering of the "blue-and-white porcelain" type—porcelain painted with cobalt blue under a clear glaze—took place in the fourteenth century, when China was under the control of the Mongols and possessed familial, economic, and diplomatic ties to porcelain centers in West Asia. The somewhat haphazard placement of the plantain, grapes, melons, and other elements on this dish reflects the style of textiles imported from the western reaches of Central Asia. The design also illustrates the complex intermingling of Chinese and West Asian styles found on early blue-and-white examples.

artworks.title: Bowl with Radiating Panels
artworks.medium: Stonepaste with pigment and gilding over glaze (Lajvardina ware)
artworks.creditLine: Gift of David M. Levitt
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: The rich surface of this bowl is covered with a rare type of glaze known as Lajvardina, after lajvard , the Persian word for lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone with gold inclusions. Found primarily in Afghanistan, lapis was treasured in the ancient world and was traded throughout West Asia to Egypt, India, and ultimately, Europe. The design painted over the blue glaze is embellished with small squares of gold leaf arranged in intricate patterns.

artworks.title: Jar
artworks.medium: Stoneware with natural ash glaze (Shigaraki ware)
artworks.creditLine: Purchased with a gift from Molly and Walter Bareiss, B.S. 1940S; the Leonard C. Hanna, Jr., Class of 1913, Fund; and the Henry Sage Goodwin, B.A. 1927, Fund
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 2nd floor, Asian Art. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: This large storage jar from the Shigaraki Valley, southeast of Kyoto, epitomizes an aesthetic integral to Japanese ceramics. Coil-built in sections, the jar demonstrates the classic Shigaraki character, which is defined by a rough, rust-orange surface combined with a natural olive-green ash glaze that runs from the narrow neck and over the bulging shoulders to the foot. The high iron content of the clay gives the body its reddish tonality, while the abundance of feldspar and quartz creates the gritty white particles on the surface. The simple form and subdued color of Shigaraki wares were cherished by tea masters; today, the jar remains eye-catching for its modest and profound beauty.

artworks.description: Prior to the mid-fourteenth century, during which the production of blue-and-white porcelain flourished, green-glazed vessels—made primarily at kilns in the south—were among the most desired and traded examples of Chinese ceramics. At the height of its popularity, the region around Longquan boasted more than two hundred kilns, making it one of the largest celadon centers in China. Unlike other such centers, which ceased production as blue-and-white gained in prominence, Longquan remained active well into the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and made significant quantities of ceramics, often for export to Southeast and West Asia.

artworks.title: Jina Chandraprabha with Other Jinas
artworks.creditLine: Gift of the Rubin-Ladd Foundation under the bequest of Ester R. Portnow

artworks.description: Like Buddhism and Hinduism, Jainism asserts that the cosmos is continuously destroyed and re-created over long periods of time. This altarpiece—which was commissioned by a man named Raja and his wife and children to benefit family members—features Chandraprabha, the eighth Jina of the current world cycle. He is surrounded by the twenty-three other Jinas of this great cosmic cycle—the current time period, before the world destroys and re-creates itself—some of whom preceded him.

artworks.description: The flute identifies this figure as Han Xiangzi, one of a group of eight quasi-historical “immortals” who became popular in twelfth-century China as the Daoist religious tradition consolidated and expanded. He is accompanied by a young attendant who holds a type of fungi known as a lingzhi , which was thought to have hallucinogenic powers and provide immortality. The feather cape worn by the attendant is a standard visual allusion to the otherworldliness of the immortals and their retinues.

artworks.description: The late fifteenth century into the early sixteenth century was a golden age for Vietnamese ceramics. The Chinese government had put prohibitions on the export of Chinese ceramics, and the Vietnamese moved quickly to fill the void in the market. The extent of this trade has become more and more apparent with the accidental discovery of shipwrecks such as the fully loaded ship discovered off Hoi An on Cu Lao Cham Island in 1993–94. The scientific excavation of the wreck took place in three campaigns between 1997 and 1999, and the Vietnamese government authorized the sale of a portion of the ceramics recovered from the site in 2000. They show the approach of Vietnamese potters to decoration in underglaze blue. The dish with overglaze enamels compares closely with those from the Hoi An cargo and demonstrates a richness of polychrome decoration unlike Chinese ceramics.

artworks.description: Before the invention of paper, all around the world stories were painted and etched onto walls, inscribed on stone and metal, and drawn on cloth, hide, and palm leaves. This wide range of media points to the universal importance and pleasure of transmitting and consuming stories in visual form. As stories began to appear on paper, they occasionally bore traces of their previous supports. For example, in this painting of a scene from the twelfth-century Persian poet Nizami’s Treasury of Secrets , the striations in the background create a texture reminiscent of a textile, and the highly stylized white clouds resemble embroidery.

artworks.description: During the late Ming period, the kilns at Jingdezhen, in Jiangxi Province, occasionally produced small, technically complex pieces for the use of the literati and wealthy merchants. This bowl has five pierced roundels set against an openwork background in the shape of Chinese coins. The characters carved in the center of the roundels are auspicious, offering wishes for longevity, wealth, health, virtue, and a peaceful death.

artworks.description: A member of the rosewood genus, huanghuali is one of the most treasured woods in Chinese culture. It is favored for its rich amber tone and the subtle figural patterns, sometimes known as ghosts, that can appear on its surface. The magnolias carved on this brush pot suggest that it was used in late winter to early summer, when the flowers of these trees, symbolic of purity and nobility, are in bloom.
