artworks.description: Plexiglas is the trade name for polymethyl methacrylate, a transparent, acrylic thermoplastic. Röhm and Haas Company, Inc., a German chemical company founded in 1907 with an American offshoot established in 1909, discovered the optically clear polymer in 1932 while researching glass laminates. This new plastic came in sheet form and could be heated, molded, and twisted without losing its clarity or strength. In 1936 Röhm and Haas began marketing the product in the United States under the name Plexiglas. About the same time, DuPont introduced a similar material called Pontalite, later renamed Lucite. Röhm and Haas hired industrial designer Gilbert Rohde to plan their exhibit at the 1939 New York World’s Fair. Housed in the Hall of Industrial Science, the exhibit educated visitors on the technical properties of Plexiglas and displayed applications of the material, including this chair. A minimal structural frame of tubular steel supports a smooth, curving sheet of Plexiglas that melds Rohde’s interests in ergonomics with the production capabilities of the material. artworks.description: Danger, Construction Ahead shows a sentinel-lined bridge abruptly ending at a sharp point. In 1940, when Kay Sage painted this otherworldly landscape, she had just returned to her native United States after a long period abroad. Later that year, she married the Surrealist painter Yves Tanguy, who aided her transition from life in Italy and Paris to New York. The clear highlight of her first solo exhibition in New York, this painting began a prolific phase in Sage's work of "intuitive sceneries," in which the imagination shaped all.

artworks.description: In 1941 the Museum of Modern Art awarded this lamp by Peter Pfisterer first prize for lighting in the museum's Organic Design exhibition. Many different kinds of light could be ingeniously obtained through the two horizontally rotating arms, on which are rotating shades. One arm could be adjusted near a chair for reading and the other could provide ambient light for the room. Pfisterer's design is a forerunner of the ubiquitous floor-to-ceiling pole lamps of the 1950s and 1960s.

artworks.description: With Austrian crystals in short supply during World War II, jewelry manufacturers sought out new materials to catch the eye of consumers. Patented by DuPont in 1937, Lucite was a lightweight, transparent, thermoplastic resin that came in a variety of colors. Its translucent shine leant an appealing opalescence and resembled the more costly moonstone. During World War II, Trifari converted some of their factories to produce Lucite windshields and turrets for fighter planes. Alfred Philippe, the company's chief designer suggested that the staff cut the imperfect discards into small cabochons for costume jewelry. Trifari produced a line of "Jelly Bellies," a menagerie of animals whose bodies were formed with these Lucite pieces. The jewelry debuted in the fall of 1943. The "Leaping Fish" lapel pin was designed and patented in 1941 by renowned industrial designer Norman Bel Geddes. Trifari added it to the "Jelly Bellies" line in the fall of 1944. In recent years, Trifari has reissued the pin; these new versions have blue rhinestones on the fish's head.

artworks.description: Before Mark Rothko developed his well-known style of painting canvases with layered fields of luminous color, he spent more than a decade producing figurative work. This canvas is one of many that reference elements from the New Testament, Greco-Roman mythology, or ancient Greek drama. Here, Rothko filled each register with motifs inspired by Greek theater and classical architecture, such as masks and a spiral design. Rothko began to develop a deep interest in the arts and aesthetics of the ancient world after reading Friedrich Nietzsche’s book Birth of Tragedy (1872). As Rothko explained, theater and mythology presented a way—what he considered the way at the time—for art to relate to its audience: "Without monsters and gods, art cannot enact our drama."

artworks.description: Georges Braque was one of the major twentieth century European artists whose career spanned several decades and embraced some of the major modern art movements, notably Fauvism and Cubism. He developed Cubism together with Pablo Picasso in the first quarter of the twentieth century, experimenting with fragmentation and multiple perspectives. Braque returned to a more figurative approach in his work in the following decades. He concentrated on interior scenes and ordinary objects by giving them a monumental presence. Le poêle (The Stove), which Braque painted during the German occupation of France during World War II, shows random household items— a waste paper basket, a bucket of coal, a table, and a stove—in his studio in Paris. The intimate scene also includes a palette on the table, as if left there by the artist. The stove—which also gives its name to the painting—seems to fill the room with heat and light, which are implied by the warm yellow and ocher color used in the background.

artworks.description: During World War II, Fernand Léger fled Nazi-occupied Paris for the United States, and he spent the war years traveling and teaching across the country, notably at Mills College, in California. He participated in the 1942 Artists in Exile exhibition at Pierre Matisse Gallery in New York, together with other exiled artists. In this painting, Léger captures the energy and dynamism of modern life that he experienced in New York, where he was fascinated by the skyscrapers and bright neon signs on Broadway. He translates this vibrancy into whirling forms and large bands of primary colors that swirl on the surface, free from the restrictions of geometric shapes and lines that characterize Léger’s earlier Cubist-influenced works.

artworks.description: Edward Hopper’s paintings of buildings are portraits, in which the human presence is implied but not seen. In Rooms for Tourists , Hopper portrays the exterior of a boarding house in Provincetown, Massachusetts. He made study drawings of the building and then traveled there repeatedly at night while he worked on the painting. The contrast between the warm, electrically lit interior and the darkness of night outside captures the sense of transience and impermanence inherent in the boarding house’s impersonal arrivals and departures .

artworks.description: By the 1940s, untrained artists had begun to be embraced by the art world, while its tastemakers were simultaneously searching for art that embodied modernity and distinctly American qualities. This celebration of "Americanness," in part, prompted some influential New York galleries to represent African American artists, such as Horace Pippin. At the Downtown Gallery, the premier commercial venue for contemporary American art, Edith Halpert helped to shape a successful career for Pippin. In 1945, the artist contributed Saturday Night Bath to a critically acclaimed group show at the Downtown Gallery, which also featured Charles Sheeler, Georgia O’Keeffe, Stuart Davis, Ralston Crawford, Ben Shahn, and George L. K. Morris, among other famous figures of American modernism.

artworks.description: Midcentury jeweler Art Smith was renowned for his wearable sculpture, and he considered the body to be fundamental to his work. His iconic Half and Half necklace plays with positive and negative space, at once hiding and exposing the skin, and the artist created further dimensionality in the piece by raising sections of the necklace off the body. The looping asymmetrical and biomorphic elements were inspired by Surrealism. Material was also important to Smith, and much of his work is made of brass, which has strong connections to African art and history.

artworks.description: The New England Glass Work, founded in 1911, reorganized in 1938 to become Rice-Weiner & Company, a manufacturer of premium costume jewelry. In 1946 the founders split the firm, with Alvin and Robert Rice establishing Barclay Jewelry, Inc., and Alexander Weiner continuing to run Rice-Weiner. The company's head designer, Louis Mark, followed the Rices to Barclay, so Weiner hired a series of high-profile outside designers to generate continued interest in the company. The best known of these designers was Norman Bel Geddes. Bel Geddes, famed for his utopian and futuristic designs for theater and industry, brought valuable name-recognition to Rice-Weiner. His jewelry was part of the Jeray line and embodied what he called "flow motion." "Yesterday's jewelry was splendid for yesterday's needs," Bel Geddes told the Hartford Courant in 1950. "Today's antique was yesterday's modern design. But with 'flow motion' in dress and figure, it was inevitable that flow motion in jewelry should develop—flexibility rather than stiffness." The overlapping arcs that make up these earrings convey a sense of motion that relates to Bel Geddes's comments. Pieces in the line were finished in gold or rhodium

artworks.description: During World War II, Richard James worked as an engineer for the U.S. Navy, developing a horsepower meter for battleships. After observing how a tension spring bounced after falling, James got the idea of transforming the industrial material into a toy. His wife, Betty, suggested the name Slinky , derived from the Swedish word for sinuous . The Jameses founded the James Spring & Wire Company (soon renamed James Industries) to fabricate the toys, which debuted at Gimbel's in Philadelphia during Christmas 1945 and nationally at the American Toy Fair in 1946. The blue-black tempered steel of this example dates it to the first years of production. It also survives with its original packaging.

artworks.description: The popularity of ranch-style and open-plan houses in the post–World War II period led to a renewed interest in freestanding screens. Ray and Charles Eames produced a screen that was ideally suited to modern taste and that had little formal relationship to the screens used in late nineteenth-century homes. Their design, the Folding Screen Wood , consisted of a series of panels of bent plywood linked by canvas webbing. The sections could move forward or backward, allowing the screen to take on an infinite variety of shapes. The undulating lines echoed contemporary sculpture and freeform design. This example was originally used in a student space at the University of California, Los Angeles.

artworks.description: Hedda Sterne fled to New York in 1941 after narrowly escaping a massacre of Romanian Jews in Bucharest. In the 1950s, the artist depicted her new surroundings in various abstract paintings. In these canvases, the structure, speed, and motion of the city are invoked in abstract, overlapping forms that seem to be in continuous movement. Here, the dynamic lines of the painting are enhanced by the round (tondo) format of the painting. Paintings like these demonstrate the active role that Sterne played in the dissemination of Abstract Expressionism. Indeed, in 1950 Life magazine named Sterne one of the best artists under age thirty-six, recognizing her innovative style. (Many publications had wrongly listed her birth year as 1916, an error she only corrected much later.)

artworks.description: Edith Heath was an early member of the craft revival that blossomed in the years directly following World War II. Heath saw the possibilities of wedding craft practices with small-scale industrial production and founded Heath Ceramics, in Sausalito, California, in 1948. Her interest in manufacturing caused her to be shunned by other studio potters, but her ceramics were a commercial success. Around 1952 she experimented with new glazes and produced a faulty glaze that was mottled green and beige. Although it was an accident, she appreciated its appearance and dubbed it Sea 'n Sand . The imperfect surfaces and earthy coloration resonated with American consumers who wanted increasingly casual housewares, and Sea 'n Sand became widely popular. A similar cruet set was advertised in a Chicago newspaper in 1953, underscoring the national appeal of Heath's designs.

artworks.description: In the late 1940s, Hall China approached Eva Zeisel about creating a line of dishes. Zeisel produced two lines: Tomorrow's Classic and Century . These lines went on to become among the most successful china patterns of the 1950s. The Tomorrow's Classic pattern included this exuberant gravy boat and spoon, which are the most daring designs in the pattern and show contemporary interests in organic design. To Zeisel's form was added Fantasy decoration, a swirl of lines punctuated by gold dots. Although the design's name is vague, it clearly draws from nuclear imagery of atoms swirling around a core.

artworks.description: A leader in midcentury avant-garde jewelry design, Peter Macchiarini was interested in the idea of hidden truths and designed the layered links of this bracelet to give the impression of windows revealing secret worlds. The bracelet is composed of square segments with biomorphic shapes cut into them, exposing a greenish-blue, patinated cavity. Additional layers and misaligned organic cuts are visible within each cavity, some featuring plateaulike structures, creating a sense of depth and mystery. Macchiarini made several bracelets in this style; other examples feature design elements inspired by Cubism and abstract art.

artworks.description: The Swiss-born and Paris-based artist Alberto Giacometti transformed post-World War II European sculpture by revolutionizing spatial perception and scale. The extreme fragility and thinness of the sculptures he made after the war express the anxiety and trauma of those years. They illustrate the artist’s fascination for the human body as well as his formal search for verticality and balance. The elongated, almost skeletal figure of his Femme debout (Standing Woman) seems to be bare of muscles and flesh, and yet is forcefully expressive at the same time.

artworks.description: Lesson One originated from what Stuart Davis called "the dynamic American scene" and, in particular, "the landscape and boats of Gloucester, Mass." At the left, flat areas of color allude to trees, buildings, and boats. Davis incorporated letters and words for design purposes, but he also used them to amplify his theoretical ideas. He inscribed "Speed" at the lower right to assert that a painting must have the impact of a billboard glimpsed from a fast-moving car. Davis declared that his inspiration came from "speeds, sounds, communications, and jazz in general."

artworks.description: From the time he was a young man, Edward Hopper was intrigued by people in urban restaurants, where strangers had little interaction. Sunlight in a Cafeteria captures an unsettling tension between the man and woman who are clearly aware of, but do not acknowledge, each other’s presence. This edgy stillness suggests the closed lines of communication in much of modern urban life. As in so many of Hopper’s paintings, the ambiguity in the scene opens up multiple narrative possibilities.

artworks.description: Of the many commercial manufacturers of pewter in the twentieth century, the firm of Reed & Barton consistently produced the most original designs with the highest quality workmanship. John A. Prip, the designer of this teapot and a central figure in modern American design, came from a family of Danish metalworkers. In addition to designing and crafting pieces for Reed & Barton, Prip also served as an instructor at the Rhode Island School of Design, in Providence. The rounded, organic belly of the pot and the crescent moon finial on the lid of this tea-and-coffee set are elements of the organic, Scandinavian-influenced style that became popular in postwar America. The black plastic cording wrapped around the handles serves not only as a decorative element but also as heat insulation.

artworks.description: Beginning in 1947, the Nelson design office developed a series of new clocks for the Howard Miller Company. Having no traditional clockface or numbers, the clocks were considered radically modern. The wall was the ground, and the clock became part of the architecture rather than an unrelated hanging object. This model is often referred to as the "Atomic Clock" because the rods and balls evoke the familiar emblem of atomic structure.

artworks.description: San Francisco–native Beatrice Wood studied drama and dance in Paris, where she met Marcel Duchamp in 1916. The French Dadaist encouraged her to draw and they collaborated on projects, but it was a fascination for luster pottery, first spied in a Dutch antiques store, that would become her lifelong pursuit. Returning to the United States, Wood sought out teachers in Glen Lukens, Vivika and Otto Heino, and émigrés Gertrud and Otto Natzler. Her simple, elegant vessels, recalling ancient ceremonial forms, explore the lustrous effects of metallic oxides in the glaze. This bowl, with its wide mouth tapering to a small foot, provides an ideal vehicle for showing variations within the textured gray glaze and represents the midpoint of her career.

artworks.description: Arline M. Fisch completed this brooch just prior to beginning her experiments with the metal textile structures for which she is now recognized. Inlaid with bone, ebony, and walnut, the brooch is one of a series of works inspired by ancient Egyptian, Etruscan, and Mayan ritual objects that Fisch encountered in museums and during her travels. The gridded layout also reflects the popularity of minimal geometric forms in the mid-twentieth century. Conscious of the motion of the wearer, Fisch suspended asymmetrical silver drops from a bar, allowing them to move and scatter reflected light.

artworks.description: In the early 1970s, Stephen Hogbin developed a conceptual approach to turning that was innovative. This chair is the most important result of those early experiments. artworks.description: Danish-born Tage Frid influenced generations of craftsmen though his woodworking courses and his three-volume Tage Frid Teaches Woodworking, which has been in continuous publication since 1979. The three-legged stool was one of Frid's most successful designs and one he used as an example in the volume dedicated to furniture making. While sitting on a fence at a horse show, Frid was inspired to explore the minimal amount of structure needed to support a grown human. The result was a stool with a seat sixteen inches wide and six inches deep. It was made in three heights; this one is the tallest. A fastidious craftsman, Frid employed a range of construction techniques to create the stool: the back and seat are sawn and shaped; the back is dovetailed to the seat; the legs and stretchers are shaved; and the legs are attached to the seat using through-tenons.

artworks.description: In 1986, the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis held the exhibition The Architecture of Frank Gehry . The dramatic installation transfixed the public and brought wide attention to the architect's work. Building off the excitement surrounding the exhibition, Gehry worked with the avant-garde housewares company Swid Powell to produce a dishware pattern, a centerpiece bowl, and candlesticks. None went beyond the design stage. These are the prototypes for the candlesticks and appear like miniature versions of Gehry's architecture. The stacked forms—based on rectangles and wedges—as well as the contrasting materials recall the Winton Guest House that Gehry was just completing near Lake Minnetonka, Minnesota.

artworks.description: Martin Wong’s La Vida is a large, celebratory depiction of the poor, vibrant, largely black and Puerto Rican neighborhood that was the Lower East Side—or Loisaida — in the 1980s. Evoking the portrait drawings the artist made and sold for a living early in his career, La Vida is populated with the faces of local residents, artists, musicians, and poets —as well as popular figures such as film star Mr. T (visible on the lower right). These characters fill the tenement windows, which Wong renders brick by brick in a fashion characteristic of his oeuvre. Many are clearly identifiable as members of the artist’s social and artistic community, including graffiti artists DAZE, Sharp, LA2, as well as poet and writer Amiri Baraka. Perhaps most importantly, Wong’s lover, collaborator, and supporter, poet and playwright Miguel Piñero, appears in the painting three times. Made only a few months after Piñero’s death, La Vida is not only a powerful and playful depiction of a neighborhood, but is also a joyful commemoration of the poet and local figurehead who insisted in his A Lower Eastside Poem : ". . . let all eyes be dry when they scatter my ashes thru the Lower Eastside."

artworks.description: The bursts of light that appear when one’s eyes are closed tightly are known as "phosphenes." For Joan A. Parcher, this optical phenomenon recalls her childhood home, where discarded lenses from a nearby glass factory were scattered across the landscape. Parcher, an experienced enamelist, was inspired to invent Reflective Glass—a type of vitreous enamel on copper—to give permanence to this experience. The pebble-like texture of her enamel easily catches the light, enhancing the reflectivity of the material. The hexagon shape is constructed from individual triangles that are connected by a flexible grid, which allows for movement and generates additional sparkle.

artworks.description: John Iversen explores the ancient technique of "nature casting" in his jewelry. This brooch is cast in bronze from a spruce leaf, and its desiccated structure is accentuated by the black patination. Throughout the year, Iversen selects leaves from around his Long Island studio, which imbue his castings with time and geography. This brooch finds beauty in the partially decayed leaf, transforming it into a meditation of the ethereality of nature. artworks.description: Harnessing the formal properties of familiar objects, Tony Feher devised a distinctive approach to sculpture that combined Minimalist strategies of symmetry, seriality, and geometry with the subject of his experience as an HIV-positive gay man during the AIDS crisis. Representative of his simple, poetic arrangements of everyday materials , Red Pair Waiting comprises two glass water bottles and a wooden block that Feher likely scavenged on walks around New York. He intended his works as open-ended propositions for viewers to interpret based on their own experiences, ideas, and memories. For example, this sculpture might suggest a couple (through its doubling), AIDS (through the red liquid), the longing for a lost beloved (through its title)—or something altogether different.

artworks.description: Born in Paris, raised on Martinique, and now living back in Paris, Julien Creuzet explores themes of migration, Black French-Caribbean identity, and cultural intermixing, or "creolization . " This sculpture features his characteristic use of brightly colored , everyday materials like fraying plastic rope, scraps of fabric, and hand-molded putty. The dynamic form shifts depending on air currents and the viewer’s position , allowing glimpses of the outline of a figure within its largely abstract design. The work’s poetic title reflects Creuzet’s aim to leave meaning open-ended. It also recalls the spirit of what Martinican writer Édouard Glissant called the "right to opacity," by which marginalized individuals and groups might refrain from offering explanation.

artworks.description: Woody De Othello explores the emotional underpinnings of everyday objects by arranging disparate items in unexpected combinations. He often represents inanimate objects through an anthropomorphizing lens, such as this wristwatch paired with a set of human lungs. Othello’s preference for hand-sculpted forms and bright glazes reflects his interest in the twentieth - century history of ceramics in the Bay Area, where he currently lives. At the same time, his work is shaped by his study of African art, such as Congolese nkisi power figures. Othello, whose parents came to the United States from Haiti, describes exploring African cultures as a way to reconnect to ancestral knowledge that has been lost in the diaspora.

artworks.description: Teresa Baker’s hybrid approach to painting combines references to her Indigenous culture with abstract forms and nontraditional materials. Here, she used spray paint, yarn, and willow (a wood employed in Mandan and Hidatsa societies to construct baskets and semisubterranean earthlodges) on a ground of artificial turf to make a schematic landscape. Her color palette recalls the Northern Plains of the United States, where she was raised. The artist’s father, Gerard Baker, was the first Native American superintendent for several national parks, including Chickasaw, Little Bighorn Battlefield, and Mount Rushmore. His commitment to incorporating Indigenous perspectives into the telling of history is a legacy that runs through Teresa Baker’s art making. As she explained, her work is "a form of storytelling . . . formally, in the way shapes, color, and textures work together to create their own language . . . and personally, because of my history with place and memory, and how the materials I use represent culture both traditional and contemporary."

artworks.description: To create The Traumatics , Keltie Ferris covered his clothed body in linseed oil, pressed it against a painted canvas, and then applied brightly colored , powdered pigments; his own body was the tool he used to mark the canvas. Inspired by the body prints of Jasper Johns and David Hammons, Ferris makes this approach to self-portraiture his own with innovative materials and vivid color. The body print is also a response to the viewing public’s interest in his identity. As Ferris has explained, "Everyone wants to know who I am . . . They’re asking all these selfhood questions . . . The body prints are my way of saying ‘Well, if you need me, here I am.’"

artworks.description: Amy Sillman’s approach to painting combines forceful color, expressive gesture, and a serious engagement with the history of the medium. She traces her influences to Abstract Expressionists like Willem de Kooning and to the color theory of Josef Albers but has forged her own style through an "anti-heroic" method embracing experimentation and "the state of not knowing," as she puts it. Little Instrument belongs to a series inspired by the human torso, here suggested by the shoulderlike diagonals at the top corners, meant to foreground the viewer’s physical relationship to the painting. In the composition’s numerous layers, built up over the course of weeks, color defines the picture plane, delineates shapes, and creates energetic—and, for Sillman, emotional—relationships.

artworks.description: Stools and headrests have been used all over Africa as prestige items. Chiefs and important persons would sit on stools on special occasions, and both men and women of wealth and status used headrests when lying down in order to preserve their elaborate hair constructions. But, for the most part, the objects were simply displayed at public ceremonies to enhance the awesome presence of their owners. In this example, the natural bend of the tree branch is used to suggest the body of a lion with a crook in the hind leg. The combination of the lion’s body with the human head may refer to the chief’s symbolic identification with this animal.

artworks.title: The Foodeater, from the series The Bad Habits
artworks.artist: Lisa Yuskavage (American, born 1962, M.F.A. 1986)//Printer: Gregory Burnet (New York, founded 1991)//Publisher: Marianne Boesky Gallery
artworks.creditLine: Print Catalyst Program
artworks.placeNote: The Gallery lists this work as on view: 4th floor, Prints, Drawings, and Photographs. Where the room sits on this map is approximate.
artworks.description: In her figurative work, Lisa Yuskavage reflects upon the dangers of misogyny, self-deprecation, social climbing, and the constant pursuit of perfection. With bulbous breasts, a distended belly, a bouffant hairdo, and pert nose and lips, the female figure in Foodeater blurs the lines between the formal tradition of the classical nude and bawdy sexuality. In her earlier print Philadelphia (1987.12.92), Yuskavage similarly worked within and challenged artistic traditions. Like Edgar Degas, she uses the monotype to experiment with form, anatomy, and space. The sketchy marks that articulate a woman walking down a building-lined street lend the work an aesthetically and psychologically unsettling air.

artworks.artist: Marie Watt (American and Seneca, born 1967, M.F.A. 1996)//Printer and publisher: Peter and James Pettengill, Wingate Studio
artworks.medium: Four plate aquatint etching with soft ground
artworks.creditLine: Print Catalyst Program

artworks.description: “A daybook marks time and story. This print is a daybook entry of sorts.” –Marie Watt While making this print in spring 2022, Watt thought about sunrises and the experience of being immersed in the light, color, and sounds of the horizon. Only four colored inks—pink, purple, yellow, and red—were used to make this print, though their layering creates a rich range of color. Looking closely, one can see the texture of fabric where it was pressed into the soft ground covering the copperplates: the fabric on top has a tight, fine weave, whereas the one below is coarser. The impressions reveal loose, curly fibers that project from the bottom and left edges of the woven cloth. As seen here, blankets play a prominent role in many of Watt’s works as symbols for cross-cultural meaning, history, and social connection. This print was made in New Haven as part of Yale University’s Print Catalyst Program. The etched copperplates used in the process are also available for viewing in the Gallery’s James E. Duffy Study Room.
